papers.title: CLEAR: Cue Learning using Evolution for Accurate Recognition Applied to Sustainability Data Extraction
papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) image recognition is a powerful tool for extracting data from images, but accuracy depends on providing sufficient cues in the prompt - requiring a domain expert for specialized tasks. We introduce Cue Learning using Evolution for Accurate Recognition (CLEAR), which uses a combination of LLMs and evolutionary computation to generate and optimize cues such that recognition of specialized features in images is improved. It achieves this by auto-generating a novel domain-specific representation and then using it to optimize suitable textual cues with a genetic algorithm. We apply CLEAR to the real-world task of identifying sustainability data from interior and exterior images of buildings. We investigate the effects of using a variable-length representation compared to fixed-length and show how LLM consistency can be improved by refactoring from categorical to real-valued estimates …

papers.title: Development necessitates evolutionarily conserved factors
papers.abstract: Early-stage generalised transcription factors in biological development are often evolutionarily conserved across species. Here, we find for the first time that similar factors functionally emerge in an alternative medium of development. Through comprehensively analysing a Neural Cellular Automata (NCA) model of morphogenesis, we find multiple properties of the hidden units that are functionally analogous to early factors in biological development. We test the generalisation abilities of our model through transfer learning of other morphologies and find that developmental strategies learnt by the model are reused to grow new body forms by conserving its early generalised factors. Our paper therefore provides evidence that nature did not become locked into one arbitrary method of developing multicellular organisms: the use of early generalised factors as fundamental control mechanisms and the resulting necessity …

papers.title: Situating AI Agents in their World: Aspective Agentic AI for Dynamic Partially Observable Information Systems
papers.abstract: Agentic LLM AI agents are often little more than autonomous chatbots: actors following scripts, often controlled by an unreliable director. This work introduces a bottom-up framework that situates AI agents in their environment, with all behaviors triggered by changes in their environments. It introduces the notion of aspects, similar to the idea of umwelt, where sets of agents perceive their environment differently to each other, enabling clearer control of information. We provide an illustrative implementation and show that compared to a typical architecture, which leaks up to 83% of the time, aspective agentic AI enables zero information leakage. We anticipate that this concept of specialist agents working efficiently in their own information niches can provide improvements to both security and efficiency.

papers.title: Address-specific sustainable accommodation choice through real-world data integration
papers.abstract: Consumers wish to choose sustainable accommodation for their travels, and in the case of corporations, may be required to do so. Yet accommodation marketplaces provide no meaningful capability for sustainable choice: typically CO2 estimates are provided that are identical for all accommodation of the same type across an entire country. We propose a decision support system that enables real choice of sustainable accommodation. We develop a data-driven address-specific metric called EcoGrade, which integrates government approved datasets and uses interpolation where data is sparse. We validate the metric on 10,000 UK addresses in 10 cities, showing the match of our interpolations to reality is statistically significant. We show how the metric has been embedded into a decision support system for a global accommodation marketplace and tested by real users over several months with positive user …

papers.title: Automated real-world sustainability data generation from images of buildings
papers.abstract: When data on features of buildings is unavailable, the task of determining how to improve those buildings in terms of carbon emissions becomes infeasible. We show that from only a set of images, a Large Language Model with appropriate prompt engineering and domain knowledge can successfully estimate a range of building features relevant for sustainability calculations. We compare our novel image-to-data method with a ground truth comprising real building data for 47 apartments and achieve accuracy better than a human performing the same task. We also demonstrate that the method can generate tailored recommendations to the owner on how best to improve their properties and discuss methods to scale the approach.

papers.title: Development necessitates homeodomain factors
papers.abstract: Homeodomain factors are known to play important roles throughout biological development, yet it remains unknown whether the requirements of development necessitate homeodomain factors. Here, we find for the first time that homeodomain factors will functionally emerge in an alternative medium of development. Through comprehensively analysing a Neural Cellular Automata (NCA) model of morphogenesis, we find multiple properties of the hidden units that are functionally analogous to homeodomain factors in biological development. Firstly, the hidden units of our model display activity patterns similar to homeodomain factors during development. Secondly, we test the generalisation abilities of our model through transfer learning of other morphologies and find that developmental strategies learnt by the model are reused to grow new body forms, in the same way evolution reuses developmental processes to grow organisms of different morphologies. Our paper therefore shows that the principles of a homeodomain may be fundamental to development, regardless of the details of how development is being implemented.

papers.title: SCAPE: Searching conceptual architecture prompts using evolution
papers.abstract: Conceptual architecture involves a highly creative exploration of novel ideas, often taken from other disciplines as architects consider radical new forms, materials, textures and colors for buildings. While today's generative AI systems can produce remarkable results, they lack the creativity demonstrated for decades by evolutionary algorithms. SCAPE, our proposed tool, combines evolutionary search with generative AI, enabling users to explore creative and good quality designs inspired by their initial input through a simple point and click interface. SCAPE injects randomness into generative AI, and enables memory, making use of the built-in language skills of GPT -4 to vary prompts via text-based mutation and crossover. We demonstrate that compared to DALL. E 3, SCAPE enables a 67% improvement in image novelty, plus improvements in quality and effectiveness of use; we show that in just three iterations …

papers.title: Kill chaos with kindness: Agreeableness improves team performance under uncertainty
papers.abstract: Teams are central to human accomplishment. Over the past half-century, psychologists have identified the Big-Five cross-culturally valid personality variables: Neuroticism, Extraversion, Openness, Conscientiousness, and Agreeableness. The first four have shown consistent relationships with team performance. Agreeableness (being harmonious, altruistic, humble, and cooperative), however, has demonstrated a non-significant and highly variable relationship with team performance. We resolve this inconsistency through computational modelling. An agent-based model (ABM) is used to predict the effects of personality traits on teamwork, and a genetic algorithm is then used to explore the limits of the ABM in order to discover which traits correlate with best and worst performing teams for a problem with different levels of uncertainty (noise). New dependencies revealed by the exploration are corroborated by …

papers.title: The “agent-based modeling for human behavior” special issue
papers.abstract: If human societies are so complex, then how can we hope to understand them? Artificial Life gives us one answer. The field of Artificial Life comprises a diverse set of introspective studies that largely ask the same questions, albeit from many different perspectives: Why are we here? Who are we? Why do we behave as we do? Starting with the origins of life provides us with fascinating answers to some of these questions. However, some researchers choose to bring their studies closer to the present day. We are, after all, human. It has been a few billion years since our ancestors were self-replicating molecules. Thus more direct studies of ourselves and our human societies can reveal truths that may lead to practical knowledge.The articles in this special issue bring together scientists who choose to perform this kind of research. Expanded from submissions to our annual Agent-Based Modelling of Human Behaviour …

papers.title: Using a variational autoencoder to learn valid search spaces of safely monitored autonomous robots for last-mile delivery
papers.abstract: The use of autonomous robots for delivery of goods to customers is an exciting new way to provide a reliable and sustainable service. However, in the real world, autonomous robots still require human supervision for safety reasons. We tackle the real-world problem of optimizing autonomous robot timings to maximize deliveries, while ensuring that there are never too many robots running simultaneously so that they can be monitored safely. We assess the use of a recent hybrid machine-learning-optimization approach COIL (constrained optimization in learned latent space) and compare it with a baseline genetic algorithm for the purposes of exploring variations of this problem. We also investigate new methods for improving the speed and efficiency of COIL. We show that only COIL can find valid solutions where appropriate numbers of robots run simultaneously for all problem variations tested. We also show that …

papers.title: COIL: Constrained optimization in learned latent space: Learning representations for valid solutions
papers.abstract: Constrained optimization problems can be difficult because their search spaces have properties not conducive to search, e.g., multimodality, discontinuities, or deception. To address such difficulties, considerable research has been performed on creating novel evolutionary algorithms or specialized genetic operators. However, if the representation that defined the search space could be altered such that it only permitted valid solutions that satisfied the constraints, the task of finding the optimal would be made more feasible without any need for specialized optimization algorithms. We propose Constrained Optimization in Latent Space (COIL), which uses a VAE to generate a learned latent representation from a dataset comprising samples from the valid region of the search space according to a constraint, thus enabling the optimizer to find the objective in the new space defined by the learned representation …

papers.title: Evolving through the looking glass: Learning improved search spaces with variational autoencoders
papers.abstract: Nature has spent billions of years perfecting our genetic representations, making them evolvable and expressive. Generative machine learning offers a shortcut: learn an evolvable latent space with implicit biases towards better solutions. We present SOLVE: Search space Optimization with Latent Variable Evolution, which creates a dataset of solutions that satisfy extra problem criteria or heuristics, generates a new latent search space, and uses a genetic algorithm to search within this new space to find solutions that meet the overall objective. We investigate SOLVE on five sets of criteria designed to detrimentally affect the search space and explain how this approach can be easily extended as the problems become more complex. We show that, compared to an identical GA using a standard representation, SOLVE with its learned latent representation can meet extra criteria and find solutions with distance to optimal …

papers.title: From evolutionary ecosystem simulations to computational models of human behavior
papers.abstract: We have a wide breadth of computational tools available today that enable a more ethical approach to the study of human cognition and behavior. We argue that the use of computer models to study evolving ecosystems provides a rich source of inspiration, as they enable the study of complex systems that change over time. Often employing a combination of genetic algorithms and agent‐based models, these methods span theoretical approaches from games to complexification, nature‐inspired methods from studies of self‐replication to the evolution of eyes, and evolutionary ecosystems of humans, from entire economies to the effects of personalities in teamwork. The review of works provided here illustrates the power of evolutionary ecosystem simulations and how they enable new insights for researchers. They also demonstrate a novel methodology of hypothesis exploration: building a computational model that …

papers.title: Opinion amplification causes extreme polarization in social networks
papers.abstract: Extreme polarization of opinions fuels many of the problems facing our societies today, from issues on human rights to the environment. Social media provides the vehicle for these opinions and enables the spread of ideas faster than ever before. Previous computational models have suggested that significant external events can induce extreme polarization. We introduce the Social Opinion Amplification Model (SOAM) to investigate an alternative hypothesis: that opinion amplification can result in extreme polarization. SOAM models effects such as sensationalism, hype, or “fake news” as people express amplified versions of their actual opinions, motivated by the desire to gain a greater following. We show for the first time that this simple idea results in extreme polarization, especially when the degree of amplification is small. We further show that such extreme polarization can be prevented by two methods …

papers.title: T-domino: exploring multiple criteria with quality-diversity and the tournament dominance objective
papers.abstract: Real-world design problems are a messy combination of constraints, objectives, and features. Exploring these problem spaces can be defined as a Multi-Criteria Exploration (MCX) problem, whose goals are to produce a set of diverse solutions with high performance across many objectives, while avoiding low performance across any objectives. Quality-Diversity algorithms produce the needed design variation, but typically consider only a single objective. We present a new ranking, T-DominO, specifically designed to handle multiple objectives in MCX problems. T-DominO ranks individuals relative to other solutions in the archive, favoring individuals with balanced performance over those which excel at a few objectives at the cost of the others. Keeping only a single balanced solution in each MAP-Elites bin maintains the visual accessibility of the archive – a strong asset for design exploration. We illustrate our …

supervisors.project_text:
Title: Design and Development of Autoencoders to Identify Latent Space for Protein Dynamics

Supervisor 1 email address: e.rosta@ucl.ac.uk

Supervisor 2 name: Sam Martino

Supervisor 2 email address: sam.martino.20@ucl.ac.uk

Pre-Requisites:
Students with background on Data Science, Machine Learning, Biophysics or Computational Chemistry are
encouraged to apply, but it is not required. Knowledge of Python programming language is also recommended,
as well as experience in scripting and Linux/bash systems. MATLAB is also a plus, but not needed. TensorFlow
and Scikit-Learn knowledge is also valued.

Work Summary:
· Learning to perform and/or visualise MD simulation data on biomolecular systems.
· Learning to use Python for data analysis and parse MD trajectories.
· Applying ML architectures e.g., autoencoders for unsupervised classification of MD data.
· Analysis of trained ML models to understand key collective variables in the latent space.
· Use of the ML models for further sampling.
• Students are expected to send their CV along with a bit of information on their background and what experience
they previously had.

Scientific aims:
· Generate and/or parse molecular dynamics trajectories for ML input
· Apply and train ML architectures to perform unsupervised learning for conformational changes taking place in
the system
· Analyse trained ML models to extract key dynamical features

Overview:
Recent AI-based structure prediction of biological systems has shown extraordinary successes, e.g., by
Google’s AlphaFold. Understanding protein conformational sampling nevertheless is still one of the two main
development areas for large scale atomistic biomolecular simulations besides force field development. To
extract relevant collective variables that describe the key features of the protein dynamics is a challenging
task, due to the high dimensionality data driven by complex interactions. Here we will explore recent machine
learning (ML) methods to develop tools that characterise the time evolution of protein dynamics and help
predict structural changes leading to the protein function.

-----
Title: Combining Machine Learning and Molecular Dynamics Simulations for the Selection of Relevant Collective Variables

Supervisor 1 email address: e.rosta@ucl.ac.uk

Supervisor 2 name: Pedro Buigues

Supervisor 2 email address: pedro.jorro.20@ucl.ac.uk

Pre-Requisites:
Students with background on Machine Learning, Biophysical systems or Computational Chemistry is useful but
not required. Experience with Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations is helpful but not required. Knowledge of
Python programming language is also recommended, as well as experience in scripting and Linux/bash
systems. TensorFlow and Scikit-Learn knowledge is also valued.

Work Summary:
· Understanding protein unbinding processes, including elements of structural biology.
· Learn to perform MD simulations and use analysis tools to gather relevant data and create datasets
(Pymol/VMD).
· Apply data visualization to find relevant reaction coordinates for biological systems.

· Create/Improve code to automate the finding of relevant variables in protein unbinding trajectories.
· Getting familiar with Machine Learning (ML) models such as Neural Networks (MLP, RNN, LSTM
architectures) and Gradient Boosting Decision Trees (Scikit-Learn and TensorFlow).
· Evaluations and limitations of the models and their applicability.
• Students are expected to send their CV along with a bit of information on their background and what experience
they previously had.

Scientific aims:
· Parse through MD data (cartesian coordinates of millions of atoms) for further analysis.
· Develop and apply ML models to learn protein unbinding classification.
· Explore and understand the MLTSA results at the high-dimensional space.
· Implement other methodologies for relevant feature identification.

Overview:
Ligand unbinding is a vital part of drug design, Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations allow us to witness these
events at high resolution, analyse the data and find relevant information that will allow us to tweak small
molecules to alter their pharmacokinetic properties. This procedure results in large amounts of data to analyse,
which requires automated methods. This project focuses on applying and developing a Machine Learning
Transition State Analysis (MLTSA) method for MD simulations to identify the relevant features in large datasets
of the ligand unbinding events. Extensive analysis of these features can be used to better sample these
processes, to understand in detail the protein involvement, and to suggest future design for optimizing
molecules with long residence times.

-----
Title: Markov models with reinforcement learning for enhanced sampling simulations

Supervisor 1 email address: e.rosta@ucl.ac.uk

Supervisor 2 name: Balint Dudas

Supervisor 2 email address: b.dudas@ucl.ac.uk

Pre-Requisites:
Essential: Python; basic ML (PyTorch/TF or scikit-learn); numerics; comfort with Linux/CLI.
Helpful: Any of OpenMM/MD basics or RL (PPO/SAC) concepts.
Training and starter code will be provided; the project can be steered more toward RL/ML, simulation, or
statistical validation depending on the student.

Work Summary:
The student will start from existing PPO/SAC code integrating Gaussian bias potentials with Langevin
dynamics (OpenMM), where the agent learns to accelerate barrier crossings. We will (i) standardise
environments (analytical → Langevin → simple MD), (ii) refine agent interfaces (continuous actions,
entropy/clip tuning), (iii) add baselines (MFPT-driven MD) for apples-to-apples comparisons. Deliverables
include a reproducible pipeline (envs, agents, baselines, metrics), comparative plots, and a short manuscript-
style report.

Scientific aims:
Robust RL biasing on physical simulators
Stabilise PPO/SAC agents for Langevin/MD environments with continuous actions (bias
centre/width/height), curriculum difficulty, and safe-exploration constraints to prevent unphysical forces
and have a more efficient performance.
Generalise state and reward representations
Move beyond handcrafted 1D states to richer encodings (local energy/forces, short trajectory snippets,
MSM-derived slow coordinates), and compare goal-based (distance/progress) vs kinetics-aware
(MFPT/success-bonus) rewards.
Prototype scaling beyond 1D
Demonstrate transfer to a 2D model surface (e.g., double-well + orthogonal coordinate) or a minimal
biomolecular CV pair, testing multi-Gaussian or adaptive bias fields.
Enhanced simulation protocol for a biomolecular example, including protein dynamics.

Benchmark against established enhanced sampling
Head-to-head comparisons with other methods; report MFPT, barrier-crossing rate, state coverage, and
estimator variance.
Pathway validation
Validate the likelihood of obtaining an observed pathway vs unbiased mechanism.

Overview:
This project advances a reinforcement-learning (RL) framework for autonomous bias placement to
accelerate rare events in molecular simulations. Building on your prior integration of PPO/SAC/A2C with
Langevin dynamics and Markov State Models (MSMs)—where the agent optimised Gaussian bias
parameters and improved sampling efficiency on 1D analytical and Langevin benchmarks—this extension will (i)
make the method more efficient, (ii) scale it beyond toy models, and (iii) establish baselines for physically
meaningful observables, such as mechanistic pathways.

-----
Title: Biasing sampling on networks

Supervisor 1 email address: e.rosta@ucl.ac.uk

Supervisor 2 name: Fahim Faizi

Supervisor 2 email address: f.faizi.14@ucl.ac.uk

Pre-Requisites:
Good working knowledge of Matlab is required. Interest and knowledge about ML methods, Python
programming is also desirable.

Work Summary:
We will explore algorithms to bias the sampling of kinetic networks. We will use stochastic block model and
other, real data-derived networks as a starting point, and run dynamical trajectories on the network nodes
using a kinetic Monte Carlo algorithm.
We will develop measures to assess the efficiency of sampling, which will serve to identify a suitable loss
function. We will also apply bias on the network, aiming to develop a history-dependent sampling where the
bias is optimally applied. We will use ML-based optimization to determine the required bias.

Scientific aims:
Sampling problems are notoriously difficult, especially for high-dimensional systems. Here we will aim to
develop ML-assisted sampling algorithms that improve sampling by applying bias in high-dimensional

problems such as for complex networks.

-----
Title: Machine Learning–Driven Functional Classification of NTP-Processing Enzymes

Supervisor 1 email address: e.rosta@ucl.ac.uk

Supervisor 2 name: Balint Dudas

Supervisor 2 email address: b.dudas@ucl.ac.uk

Pre-Requisites:
Basic Python programming: some familiarity with data handling using libraries such as pandas, numpy,
and matplotlib.
Introductory machine learning knowledge: understanding of model training, validation, and
performance evaluation (e.g., using scikit-learn or PyTorch).
General understanding of protein structure and enzyme function (e.g., active sites, cofactors,
catalytic residues) is useful.
Helpful but not essential:
Experience with bioinformatics tools or databases (UniProt, PDB, InterPro, or AlphaFold/Protenix).
Familiarity with sequence embeddings or deep learning models for proteins (e.g., ESM, ProtBERT).
Interest in structural enzymology or computational biochemistry, particularly mechanisms of
ATP/GTP hydrolysis.
Training provided:
All domain-specific training (e.g., enzyme annotation systems, use of Protenix and DALI, feature extraction
pipelines, and model interpretation tools) will be provided during the project. The student will develop practical
skills in data curation, feature engineering, and machine learning applied to biological problems.

Work Summary:
This project will investigate how information encoded in protein sequences determines three-dimensional
structure and ultimately biochemical function. The student will use a combination of bioinformatics and
machine learning approaches to identify sequence and structural patterns that distinguish proteins with
different catalytic or binding activities. Using curated datasets from UniProt, PDB, and InterPro, the project
will integrate modern protein language models and structural prediction tools (e.g., AlphaFold or Protenix)
to derive descriptors that capture functionally relevant features such as active-site geometry, metal-ion
coordination, or ligand-binding motifs.
Machine learning models will then be trained to predict the functional class or Enzyme Commission (EC)
number of proteins from these features, and results will be benchmarked against established bioinformatics
annotation pipelines. Through this work, the student will gain experience in computational protein science,
including data curation, feature engineering, and model development, while contributing to the broader
understanding of how sequence diversity shapes protein function across enzyme families.

Scientific aims:
Uncover sequence–structure–function relationships in proteins
Identify how variations in amino acid sequence give rise to distinct structural motifs, active-site
geometries, and catalytic functions across enzyme families.
Develop computational models for protein function prediction
Build and evaluate machine learning models that integrate sequence embeddings and structural features
to classify proteins by functional category (e.g., EC number or catalytic mechanism).
Characterise structural determinants of enzymatic specificity
Determine which sequence or structural features—such as cofactor-binding motifs, metal coordination
sites, or residue conservation patterns—most strongly influence functional outcomes.

Benchmark and validate predictive approaches
Compare the performance of data-driven models against existing bioinformatics annotation tools (e.g.,
SUPFAM, InterPro, DALI) and assess their ability to predict or refine enzyme function assignments.
Enable functional annotation of uncharacterised proteins
Apply the trained models to unannotated or poorly characterised protein sequences to propose testable
hypotheses about their molecular roles, supporting future experimental validation.

Overview:
Understanding how protein sequence determines structure and function is a central challenge in molecular
biology. Despite the success of structural prediction tools such as AlphaFold, linking these predicted
structures to specific biochemical functions remains a major unsolved problem. This project aims to bridge
that gap by developing computational and machine learning approaches that connect sequence information to
protein function across diverse enzyme families.
The student will assemble and analyse large datasets of protein sequences and structures from resources
such as UniProt, PDB, and InterPro, extracting features that describe active-site geometry, residue
conservation, and cofactor-binding motifs. These data will be used to train machine learning models capable
of predicting functional classes (e.g., Enzyme Commission numbers) directly from sequence and structure-
derived descriptors.
By integrating methods from bioinformatics, data science, and computational biochemistry, the project will
provide new insights into the determinants of enzyme specificity and catalysis. The broader goal is to advance
automated protein annotation and improve our ability to predict function for the growing number of
uncharacterised proteins emerging from large-scale sequencing efforts.

-----
Title: Causal Inference and Mechanistic Discovery in Complex Time-Series Data

Supervisor 1 email address: e.rosta@ucl.ac.uk

Supervisor 2 name: Balint Dudas

Supervisor 2 email address: b.dudas@ucl.ac.uk

Pre-Requisites:
Essential skills:
Basic proficiency in Python programming and data handling (numpy, pandas, matplotlib).

Familiarity with statistics and time-series concepts (e.g., correlation, regression, or basic signal
analysis).
Interest in the principles of causality, mechanistic modeling, or complex system dynamics.
Desirable (but not essential):
Experience with machine learning or graph-based models (scikit-learn, networkx, or pytorch).
Exposure to simulation data analysis (e.g., molecular dynamics, agent-based models, or physical
simulations).
Knowledge of basic probability theory or information theory concepts (entropy, mutual information).
Training provided:
Students will receive hands-on training in causal inference algorithms, model evaluation, and scientific data
visualization. The project can be tailored to emphasize data science, physics, or biomolecular applications
depending on the student’s background and interests.

Work Summary:
This project will apply causal inference techniques to identify directional relationships within complex
biological and physical systems. While traditional data analysis methods reveal correlations between variables,
they cannot determine which processes drive others. The student will explore how causal discovery
algorithms—such as PC, PCMCI, VAR-LiNGAM, and Transfer Entropy—can be used to extract cause–effect
networks from diverse time-series data, including analytical models, publicly available datasets, and
molecular dynamics (MD) simulations.
The project will begin with controlled synthetic datasets to benchmark and validate different causal algorithms,
before extending the analysis to more complex biological and physical systems. By comparing methods and
quantifying their robustness, the student will help establish best practices for applying causal inference to
time-dependent scientific data.
Through this work, the student will gain experience in time-series analysis, causal discovery, and
computational modeling, developing transferable skills that bridge data science, physics, and molecular
biology. The project will contribute to a growing effort to move beyond correlation-based approaches and
toward mechanistic understanding of dynamic systems.

Scientific aims:
Develop and benchmark causal discovery methods for molecular systems
Evaluate and compare existing causal inference algorithms (e.g., PC, PCMCI, VAR-LiNGAM, Transfer
Entropy) using synthetic and molecular dynamics (MD) datasets to identify robust approaches for
detecting directional dependencies in biomolecular trajectories.
Quantify causal relationships between structural and dynamical variables
Apply causal inference to MD simulations to determine which molecular coordinates (residues, distances,
dihedral angles, solvent interactions) act as causal drivers of conformational transitions, binding events,
or allosteric communication.
Validate causal insights against physical and biochemical knowledge
Test the inferred causal networks against known mechanistic models of protein motion or ligand binding
to assess their physical plausibility and interpretability.
Establish a general workflow for causal analysis of biomolecular simulations
Integrate trajectory preprocessing, dimensionality reduction, causal discovery, and visualization into a
reproducible computational pipeline applicable across protein and nucleic acid systems.

Explore applications to mechanistic and drug discovery problems
Demonstrate how causal inference can reveal functionally relevant pathways, identify key residues or
water-mediated couplings, and generate hypotheses for experimental testing or structure-based design.

Overview:
Traditional molecular dynamics (MD) simulations provide rich time-resolved data on biomolecular motions but
often rely on correlation-based analyses, which cannot reveal the true direction of molecular influence. This
project applies causal discovery methods to uncover the underlying cause–effect relationships governing
protein–ligand interactions and conformational changes.
Using timeseries from databases and MD simulations, the project will benchmark several causal inference
algorithms (e.g., PC, PCMCI, Transfer Entropy, and VAR-LiNGAM) to determine their performance on
synthetic and real molecular datasets. The best-performing approach will then be applied to identify causal
pathways linking key residues and solvent molecules during ligand binding and unbinding events.
By integrating computational biophysics with causal inference and time-series analysis, the project aims
to move beyond correlations to reveal the mechanistic drivers of conformational transitions in proteins. The
broader goal is to establish general frameworks for applying causal discovery to biomolecular simulations,
ultimately providing insights relevant to drug design, allosteric regulation, and molecular mechanism
elucidation.

papers.title: Cache challenge# 2: targeting the RNA site of the SARS-CoV-2 helicase Nsp13
papers.abstract: A critical assessment of computational hit-finding experiments (CACHE) challenge was conducted to predict ligands for the SARS-CoV-2 Nsp13 helicase RNA binding site, a highly conserved COVID-19 target. Twenty-three participating teams comprised of computational chemists and data scientists used protein structure and data from fragment-screening paired with advanced computational and machine learning methods to each predict up to 100 inhibitory ligands. Across all teams, 1957 compounds were predicted and were subsequently procured from commercial catalogs for biophysical assays. Of these compounds, 0.7% were confirmed to bind to Nsp13 in a surface plasmon resonance assay. The six best-performing computational workflows used fragment growing, active learning, or conventional virtual screening with and without complementary deep-learning scoring functions. Follow-up functional assays …

papers.title: Nature counts to three: Universal Mg-pinch motif polarizes the cleaved bond in NTP-processing enzymes
papers.abstract: Phosphates are essential for all forms of life, playing key roles in DNA/RNA, signaling, energy storage and transfer, and biosynthetic processes. We conducted a quantitative analysis of nucleoside triphosphate (NTP) processing enzymes across all enzymatic reactions, revealing their dominance in phosphate reactivity with ATP as the most prevalent substrate. Two main reaction types occur predominantly: cleavage resulting in (i) pyrophosphate or (ii) phosphate release/transfer. The large majority of NTP processing enzymes require divalent Mg2+ ions in a mechanistically analogous manner. Despite their importance, the precise coordination of metal ions in the catalytically competent active site structure in many NTP processing enzymes remains elusive. We hypothesized that efficient phosphate processing requires specific metal ion coordination, facilitating the catalytic reaction. By examining a vast dataset of …

papers.title: Quantifying cooperativity through binding free energies in molecular glue degraders
papers.abstract: Molecular glues represent a novel therapeutic modality facilitating the stabilization of protein–protein interactions (PPIs), thus enabling the targeting of previously “undruggable” proteins. We develop a computational procedure to screen for molecular glues using a pathway-independent free energy calculation method for accurately assessing the cooperativity. We employ a combined ligand and protein free energy perturbation (FEP) method to calculate the cooperative effect of a ligand for ternary binding. We study the cooperative binding mechanisms of molecular glue degraders, specifically cereblon (CRBN) modulators targeting Ikaros family zinc finger 2 (IKZF2), a transcription factor implicated in cancer immunotherapy. We present a comprehensive computational protocol for screening large molecular libraries to identify potent molecular glues. By leveraging cooperative binding principles in ternary complex …

papers.title: Reaction Mechanism and Metal Selectivity of Human SAMHD1 Elucidated by QM/MM Calculations
papers.abstract: 2′-Deoxynucleoside-5′-triphosphate triphosphohydrolases (dNTPases) constitute a crucial enzyme family that plays a pivotal role in antiviral innate immunity. Among these enzymes, human SAMHD1 has emerged as a dNTPase with distinct catalytic properties and active-site architecture. This metalloenzyme regulates cellular dNTP concentration through its ability to hydrolyze all four canonical dNTPs into their corresponding 2′-deoxynucleosides and inorganic triphosphates, a reaction requiring coordinated iron and magnesium ions for enzymatic activity. In the present work, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM) calculations are employed to investigate the mechanistic details of dATP hydrolysis mediated by two metal ions. Starting from the resolved crystal structure, Model-1, containing a Fe2+ in the active site, was constructed. Our calculations …

papers.title: The need to implement FAIR principles in biomolecular simulations
papers.abstract: In the Big Data era, a change of paradigm in the use of molecular dynamics is required. Trajectories should be stored under FAIR (findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable) requirements to favor its reuse by the community under an open science paradigm.

papers.title: Classification Pipeline for Galactose Oxidase Variants Based on a Combined Transition State Molecular Dynamics and Machine Learning approach
papers.abstract: In recent years, the field of Deep Learning has progressed to the point where a lot of protein properties, especially the ones related to structure, can be predicted with high accuracy. However, catalytic properties in mutated enzymes remain notoriously difficult to predict, due to the many dimensions of the problem. Proteins for which there is scarce experimental data are particularly difficult to handle. Here we propose a combination of a physics-based approach and machine learning to try to overcome some of the limitations for experimental datasets of small size, which cannot utilize Deep Learning architectures. Galactose Oxidase is a copper oxidoreductase that enables the catalytic oxidation of D-galactose and has been the subject of a lot of research in the field of directed evolution. The wild type enzyme has been engineered to convert primary and secondary alcohols, considerably expanding the scope of the …

papers.title: Kemeny constant-based optimization of network clustering using graph neural networks
papers.abstract: The recent trend in using network and graph structures to represent a variety of different data types has renewed interest in the graph partitioning (GP) problem. This interest stems from the need for general methods that can both efficiently identify network communities and reduce the dimensionality of large graphs while satisfying various application-specific criteria. Traditional clustering algorithms often struggle to capture the complex relationships within graphs and generalize to arbitrary clustering criteria. The emergence of graph neural networks (GNNs) as a powerful framework for learning representations of graph data provides new approaches to solving the problem. Previous work has shown GNNs to be capable of proposing partitionings using a variety of criteria. However, these approaches have not yet been extended to Markov chains or kinetic networks. These arise frequently in the study of molecular …

papers.title: Kinetics-Optimized Enhanced Sampling Using Mean First Passage Times
papers.abstract: Molecular dynamics simulations have become essential in many areas of atomistic modelling from drug discovery to materials science. They provide critical atomic-level insights into key dynamical events experiments cannot easily capture. However, their impact often falls short as the timescales of the important processes are inaccessible using standard molecular dynamics. Enhanced sampling methods provided avenues to access such crucial rare events, for example key slow conformational changes of biomolecules. However, the bias in enhanced sampling simulations is rarely optimized, and even if they are, the optimization criteria is based on the thermodynamics or Hamiltonian of the system, but do not directly consider molecular kinetics. Here, we introduce a novel enhanced sampling algorithm that adaptively optimizes the bias based on the kinetics of the system for the first time. We identify the optimal bias that minimizes a key physical observable, the mean first passage time (MFPT) from a starting state to a target state. Our algorithm makes use of the relation between biased and unbiased kinetics obtained from discretized Markov state models (MSMs), as established in the dynamic histogram analysis method (DHAM). We demonstrate the applicability of the method for different 1D and 2D analytical potential-based model examples, NaCl dissociation in explicit water, and phosphate unbinding in Ras GTPase. Our algorithm has excellent performance compared with state-of-art enhanced sampling methods in terms of the timescales required to reach the final state in the benchmarking systems. Our findings provide a novel, kinetics-driven …

papers.title: Uncovering low-frequency vibrations in surface-enhanced Raman of organic molecules
papers.abstract: Accessing the terahertz (THz) spectral domain through surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) is challenging and opens up the study of low-frequency molecular and electronic excitations. Compared to direct THz probing of heterogenous ensembles, the extreme plasmonic confinement of visible light to deep sub-wavelength scales allows the study of hundreds or even single molecules. We show that self-assembled molecular monolayers of a set of simple aromatic thiols confined inside single-particle plasmonic nanocavities can be distinguished by their low-wavenumber spectral peaks below 200 cm−1, after removal of a bosonic inelastic contribution and an exponential background from the spectrum. Developing environment-dependent density-functional-theory simulations of the metal-molecule configuration enables the assignment and classification of their THz vibrations as well as the identification …

papers.title: Dynamic regulation of RAS and RAS signaling
papers.abstract: RAS proteins regulate most aspects of cellular physiology. They are mutated in 30% of human cancers and 4% of developmental disorders termed Rasopathies. They cycle between active GTP-bound and inactive GDP-bound states. When active, they can interact with a wide range of effectors that control fundamental biochemical and biological processes. Emerging evidence suggests that RAS proteins are not simple on/off switches but sophisticated information processing devices that compute cell fate decisions by integrating external and internal cues. A critical component of this compute function is the dynamic regulation of RAS activation and downstream signaling that allows RAS to produce a rich and nuanced spectrum of biological outputs. We discuss recent findings how the dynamics of RAS and its downstream signaling is regulated. Starting from the structural and biochemical properties of wild-type and …

Mechanism-based redesign of GAP to activate oncogenic Ras
papers.abstract: Ras GTPases play a crucial role in cell signaling pathways. Mutations of the Ras gene occur in about one third of cancerous cell lines and are often associated with detrimental clinical prognosis. Hot spot residues Gly12, Gly13, and Gln61 cover 97% of oncogenic mutations, which impair the enzymatic activity in Ras. Using QM/MM free energy calculations, we present a two-step mechanism for the GTP hydrolysis catalyzed by the wild-type Ras.GAP complex. We found that the deprotonation of the catalytic water takes place via the Gln61 as a transient Brønsted base. We also determined the reaction profiles for key oncogenic Ras mutants G12D and G12C using QM/MM minimizations, matching the experimentally observed loss of catalytic activity, thereby validating our reaction mechanism. Using the optimized reaction paths, we devised a fast and accurate procedure to design GAP mutants that activate G12D Ras …

papers.title: SERS sensing of dopamine with Fe (III)‐sensitized nanogaps in recleanable AuNP monolayer films
papers.abstract: Sensing of neurotransmitters (NTs) down to nm concentrations is demonstrated by utilizing self‐assembled monolayers of plasmonic 60 nm Au nanoparticles in close‐packed arrays immobilized onto glass substrates. Multiplicative surface‐enhanced Raman spectroscopy enhancements are achieved by integrating Fe(III) sensitizers into the precisely‐defined <1 nm nanogaps, to target dopamine (DA) sensing. The transparent glass substrates allow for efficient access from both sides of the monolayer aggregate films by fluid and light, allowing repeated sensing in different analytes. Repeated reusability after analyte sensing is shown through oxygen plasma cleaning protocols, which restore pristine conditions for the nanogaps. Examining binding competition in multiplexed sensing of two catecholamine NTs, DA and epinephrine, reveals their bidentate binding and their interactions. These systems are promising for …

papers.title: Strong structuring arising from weak cooperative OH··· π and CH··· O hydrogen bonding in benzene-methanol solution
papers.abstract: Weak hydrogen bonds, such as O-H···π and C-H···O, are thought to direct biochemical assembly, molecular recognition, and chemical selectivity but are seldom observed in solution. We have used neutron diffraction combined with H/D isotopic substitution to obtain a detailed spatial and orientational picture of the structure of benzene-methanol mixtures. Our analysis reveals that methanol fully solvates and surrounds each benzene molecule. The expected O-H···π interaction is highly localised and directional, with the methanol hydroxyl bond aligned normal to the aromatic plane and the hydrogen at a distance of 2.30 Å from the ring centroid. Simultaneously, the tendency of methanol to form chain and cyclic motifs in the bulk liquid is manifest in a highly templated solvation structure in the plane of the ring. The methanol molecules surround the benzene so that the O-H bonds are coplanar with the aromatic ring …

papers.title: Collective mid-infrared vibrations in surface-enhanced Raman scattering
papers.abstract: Surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) is typically assumed to occur at individual molecules neglecting intermolecular vibrational coupling. Here, we show instead how collective vibrations from infrared (IR) coupled dipoles are seen in SERS from molecular monolayers. Mixing IR-active molecules with IR-inactive spacer molecules controls the intermolecular separation. Intermolecular coupling leads to vibrational frequency upshifts up to 8 cm–1, tuning with the mixing fraction and IR dipole strength, in excellent agreement with microscopic models and density functional theory. These cooperative frequency shifts can be used as a ruler to measure intermolecular distance and disorder with angstrom resolution. We demonstrate this for photochemical reactions of 4-nitrothiophenol, which depletes the number of neighboring IR-active molecules and breaks the collective vibration, enabling direct tracking of the …

papers.title: Combined free-energy calculation and machine learning methods for understanding ligand unbinding kinetics
papers.abstract: The determination of drug residence times, which define the time an inhibitor is in complex with its target, is a fundamental part of the drug discovery process. Synthesis and experimental measurements of kinetic rate constants are, however, expensive and time consuming. In this work, we aimed to obtain drug residence times computationally. Furthermore, we propose a novel algorithm to identify molecular design objectives based on ligand unbinding kinetics. We designed an enhanced sampling technique to accurately predict the free-energy profiles of the ligand unbinding process, focusing on the free-energy barrier for unbinding. Our method first identifies unbinding paths determining a corresponding set of internal coordinates (ICs) that form contacts between the protein and the ligand; it then iteratively updates these interactions during a series of biased molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to reveal the ICs …

papers.title: In-Situ Spectro-Electrochemistry of Conductive Polymers Using Plasmonics to Reveal Doping Mechanisms
papers.abstract: Conducting polymers are a key component for developing wearable organic electronics, but tracking their redox processes at the nanoscale to understand their doping mechanism remains challenging. Here we present an in-situ spectro-electrochemical technique to observe redox dynamics of conductive polymers in an extremely localized volume (<100 nm3). Plasmonic nanoparticles encapsulated by thin shells of different conductive polymers provide actively tuned scattering color through switching their refractive index. Surface-enhanced Raman scattering in combination with cyclic voltammetry enables detailed studies of the redox/doping process. Our data intriguingly show that the doping mechanism varies with polymer conductivity: a disproportionation mechanism dominates in more conductive polymers, while sequential electron transfer prevails in less conductive polymers.

papers.title: Molecular vibration explorer: An online database and toolbox for surface-enhanced frequency conversion and infrared and Raman spectroscopy
papers.abstract: We present Molecular Vibration Explorer, a freely accessible online database and interactive tool for exploring vibrational spectra and tensorial light-vibration coupling strengths of a large collection of thiolated molecules. The “Gold” version of the database gathers the results from density functional theory calculations on 2800 commercially available thiol compounds linked to a gold atom, with the main motivation to screen the best molecules for THz and mid-infrared to visible upconversion. Additionally, the “Thiol” version of the database contains results for 1900 unbound thiolated compounds. They both provide access to a comprehensive set of computed spectroscopic parameters for all vibrational modes of all molecules in the database. The user can simultaneously investigate infrared absorption, Raman scattering, and vibrational sum- and difference-frequency generation cross sections. Molecules can be …

papers.title: Optical suppression of energy barriers in single molecule-metal binding
papers.abstract: Transient bonds between molecules and metal surfaces underpin catalysis, bio/molecular sensing, molecular electronics, and electrochemistry. Techniques aiming to characterize these bonds often yield conflicting conclusions, while single-molecule probes are scarce. A promising prospect confines light inside metal nanogaps to elicit in operando vibrational signatures through surface-enhanced Raman scattering. Here, we show through analysis of more than a million spectra that light irradiation of only a few microwatts on molecules at gold facets is sufficient to overcome the metallic bonds between individual gold atoms and pull them out to form coordination complexes. Depending on the molecule, these light-extracted adatoms persist for minutes under ambient conditions. Tracking their power-dependent formation and decay suggests that tightly trapped light transiently reduces energy barriers at the metal …

Title: Partial Volume Correction in PET Imaging of the Lung

Supervisor 1 email address: k.thielemans@ucl.ac.uk

Supervisor 2 name: Kjell Erlandsso

Pre-Requisites:
Programming experience essential, ideally Python. Basic knowledge of CNN architectures and training desired
but not required. Interest of making meaningful contributions to research.

Work Summary:
The work involved will consist of simulation of realistic PET images for the thorax to evaluate different PVC
methods. If adaptations of PVC methods are required, the student will need to implement them using the SIRF
open source software using Python. We will also
have 3D printed test objects available. The student can participate in scanning the test objects and data
analysis.
• Email with brief CV. Short meeting to discuss interests and background

Scientific aims:
This project will investigate if some these techniques can be adapted to the lung, which has several challenges
including air content and heterogeneous uptake.

Overview:
Positron Emission Tomography (PET) imaging is a common technique to image functional processes. By
injecting a radiotracer, metabolic processes related to that molecule can be measured in vivo. There is
increasing interest in imaging the diseased lung, with projects at UCL/H including post-COVID-19 scanning
with multiple radiotracers.
However, due to the physics processes involved in doing the PET measurement as well limitations on
(radioactive) dose to the patient, spatial resolution of PET is limited to about 5mm in the thorax. For certain
radionuclides, positron range degrades the resolution even more, especially in the lung due to its low density.
This reduced spatial resolution impacts quantification and is called the “partial volume effect” (PVE).
Several techniques have been developed to correct for PVE, ranging from model-based, deconvolution to
machine learning using convolutional neural networks [1]. However, these techniques have mostly been
developed for, and evaluated in, brain application.
This project will be working within a research framework on standardisation of lung imaging with PET in a
collaboration between the Institute of Nuclear Medicine at UCL/UCLH and the UK National Physical Laboratory.
[1] Erlandsson, Kjell, Irène Buvat, P. Hendrik Pretorius, Benjamin A. Thomas, and Brian F. Hutton. ‘A Review of
Partial Volume Correction Techniques for Emission Tomography and Their Applications in Neurology,
Cardiology and Oncology’. Physics in Medicine and Biology 57, no. 21 (November 2012): R119–59.
https://doi.org/10.1088/0031-9155/57/21/r119 .

Title: Using Deep Learning to estimate average PET sensitivity to correct for motion in PET

Supervisor 1 email address: k.thielemans@ucl.ac.uk

Supervisor 2 name: Sam Porter

Supervisor 2 email address: sam.porter.18@ucl.ac.uk

Pre-Requisites:
Programming experience essential, ideally Python or MATLAB. Basic knowledge of CNN architectures for
imaging and training desired but not required. Interest of making meaningful contributions to research.

Work Summary:
In Positron Emission Tomography (PET) a radiotracer is injected and its distribution is measured, allowing to
investigate metabolic processes related to that molecule in vivo. In the thorax, patient motion is unavoidable in
standard clinical scans due to the scan duration (~2 minutes). Several methods have been developed to
correct the motion by splitting data in different motion states and taking motion into account during
reconstruction. However, as the measured photons are attenuated, the effective sensitivity varies locally as
well as with motion. This needs to be taken into account, but the relevant calculation is often the most
computationally expensive part.
The aim of this project is to investigate the use of CNNs to compute how the effective sensitivity changes with
motion. This is a novel approach and could lead to publication.

Title: Using machine learning techniques to denoise SPECT images for quantitative accuracy

Supervisor 1 email address: k.thielemans@ucl.ac.uk

Supervisor 2 name: Cate Gascoigne

Supervisor 2 email address: cate.cascoigne.23@ucl.ac.uk

Pre-Requisites:
Programming experience and a basic understanding of machine learning is essential. An interest in medical
imaging and quantitative analysis is desirable.

Overview:
Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT) is a three-dimensional medical imaging technique. A
radiopharmaceutical ‘tracer’ is administered to the patient and accumulates in organs or processes under
investigation. For example, radiopharmaceuticals which bind to proteins found on certain types of tumours can
be used to detect and evaluate cancer. Gamma photons emitted by the tracer can be detected outside the
body using a gamma camera. This information is converted into a three-dimensional image representing the
distribution of the tracer, allowing clinicians to infer functional information. This can help to diagnose the
patient’s condition, monitor disease progression and assess the effectiveness of any treatments.
For many years, clinical evaluation of SPECT images has been mainly qualitative, i.e. clinicians report what they
can see in the images without access to quantitative metrics. Improvements in technology and advances the
development of cancer treatments have led to increased interest in quantitative SPECT imaging. This allows
clinicians to estimate absolute quantities of tracer uptake within volumes of interest. This is useful for
assessing the extent of disease, planning treatments and comparing uptake between timepoints to evaluate
progression.
Due to limitations associated with SPECT, image quality can be poor, and quantification is inaccurate. Low
spatial resolution and low sensitivity (the proportion of gamma photons emitted which contribute to the final
image) lead to blurry and noisy images. It is difficult to distinguish structures from the background and
estimate their true size and tracer concentration. Traditionally, image quality has been understood as a
compromise between spatial resolution and sensitivity. However, machine learning (ML) introduces the
possibility of overcoming this trade-off.
This project will focus on using state-of-the-art ML techniques to denoise SPECT images and achieve
quantitative accuracy, particularly in small volumes of interest. The work will build on two recent projects which
our group has participated in. The first project compared the denoising performance of three models (a 3D U-

Net, a projection-domain single-step PDPM (Poisson diffusion-based 3D U-Net), and Swin UNETR) on
simulated and clinical data. The second project trained a 2D U-Net to denoise simulated and clinical data and
assessed quantitative accuracy in small volumes (tumours). Possible areas to expand the research include:
· Generating a large, diverse and clinically realistic training dataset, for example using Monte Carlo
simulation.
· Investigating model architectures, hyperparameters, loss functions and training strategies to overcome the
class imbalance that arises because volumes of interest are only a small proportion of the total image volume.
This project will use open-source image simulation and reconstruction software.

References:
Hutton, B. F.; Erlandsson, K.; Thielemans, K. Quantification in Emission Tomography. In Handbook of
Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging for Physicists; CRC Press, 2022; Vol. 1.
Balaji, V.; Song, T.-A.; Malekzadeh, M.; Heidari, P.; Dutta, J. Artificial Intelligence for PET and SPECT Image
Enhancement. Journal of Nuclear Medicine 2023. https://doi.org/10.2967/jnumed.122.265000.
